notable_claims: The NZ anti-porn law defines 'publication' to include any electronic storage capable of being reproduced as a word or representation.
Possession of objectionable material is an offense regardless of whether the defendant had knowledge that the material was objectionable.
University administrators may engage in self-censorship to avoid fines (up to $5,000 for corporate bodies) and criminal records resulting from automated news feeds.
classification.summary: Peter Gutmann discusses how a draconian New Zealand anti-pornography law influenced the University of Canterbury's decision to censor newsgroups. He argues that the law's broad definition of 'publication' and strict liability for possession make university network administrators vulnerable to severe fines and criminal charges for hosting automated Usenet feeds. The post highlights the tension between national morality laws and the technical reality of uncontrolled data flow on early academic networks.
